newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's lead disappears in Georgia - poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's lead disappears in Georgia - poll.

text.p: President Clinton's once comfortable lead over Republican challenger Bob Dole has all but disappeared in Georgia, one of the four Southern states Clinton carried in 1992, according to an opinion poll published Friday.

Clinton, who led Dole by 15 percentage points a month ago, had only a three-point lead on the Republican in the latest survey of 925 likely voters. Given a three-point margin of error, the results showed the two contenders to be in a statistical dead heat.
The poll put Clinton's support at 43 percent, with Dole at 40 percent and Texas billionaire Ross Perot at eight percent. The number of undecided voters was 10 percent.
The survey was conducted Oct. 26-30 by Marketing Workshop Inc. for the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and WSB-TV, ABC's affiliate in Atlanta.

The same poll showed a similar turn in the Senate race in Georgia, where Democrat Max Cleland trailed Republican Guy Millner by 47-45 percent. In a Marketing Workshop survey published a month ago, Cleland had led Millner by 16 points.
Meanwhile, the results showed Dole to be benefiting from a closing gender gap, with women increasingly being drawn into the Republican camp.
But the erosion of Clinton's lead was almost entirely among white voters, only one in three of whom said they planned to vote for the president. Black voters remained overwhelmingly loyal to him.

The newspaper quoted political experts as saying the racial patterns reflected by the survey were similar to those seen in the 1992 and 1994 elections, meaning that voter turnout would be crucial for the two candidates.
In 1992, Clinton carried Georgia by a narrow margin. He also took Arkansas, Louisiana and Tennessee, among Southern states.
